start.text: Hey! I'm Vishan. This setup is used to study how people move and interact with their environment.

main2.text: We used equipment like this in our Work Design and Ergonomics class to study how people perform different tasks.

main3.text: One thing we can study is where a person is looking. Eye-tracking data helps show what grabs their attention during a task.

main4.text: Ergonomics can also look at body position and movement. We want to understand how someone physically performs their work.

choices.label: That makes a lot of sense.

main5.text: Engineers can use that information to identify awkward or inefficient ways of working and improve the task or workspace.

choices.label: Can you give me an example?

main6.text: The goal is to design work around the person. A good ergonomic design can make a task easier and more comfortable to perform.

choices.label: That's a smart way to design.
How would an engineer improve a task?

main7.text: So this equipment helps turn human behavior into data engineers can study when designing better workplaces and systems.

choices.label: Why do engineers need human data?

main8.text: And that's the basic idea! Ergonomics combines people, data, and engineering to help design work that fits the user.

tracking.text: The setup can help study things like visual attention and human movement while someone performs a task.

choices.label: What do you mean by visual attention?

visual_attention.text: Visual attention is basically where someone focuses while doing something. Eye tracking lets us analyze those patterns.

ergonomics.text: Ergonomics is about designing tasks, tools, and workplaces around people instead of forcing people to adapt to poor designs.

choices.label: Can you give me an example?

eye_tracking.text: Eye tracking can show where someone looks and how their attention moves during a task. That can reveal confusing or inefficient designs.

choices.label: What would that look like in real life?

eye_example.text: Imagine using a control panel. Eye tracking could show whether important information is easy to find or constantly being missed.

body_movement.text: Body position can reveal awkward reaching, bending, or movement patterns. Those patterns may suggest the workspace needs improvement.

example.text: Imagine someone repeatedly reaching too far for a tool. An engineer could redesign the workstation so the tool is easier to reach.

choices.label: How would you know there's a problem?

problem_detection.text: Engineers can combine observations and measured data. Repeated awkward motions or inefficient behavior can point to a design problem.

choices.label: What happens after they find a problem?

improvements.text: They might change the workstation height, move tools closer, adjust a display, or redesign how the task is performed.

choices.label: How do they know the change worked?

testing.text: They can test the redesigned task and collect data again. Then they compare the results to see whether the design improved.

iteration.text: Exactly! Engineers test, learn, redesign, and test again. Here, the difference is that the human user is part of the system.

choices.label: Why is the person part of the system?

human_factors.text: Because a technically good system can still fail if it's uncomfortable or confusing for the person who has to use it.

choices.label: Is that what human factors means?

human_factors2.text: Pretty much! Human factors studies how people interact with tools, technology, environments, and systems.

choices.label: How does ergonomics fit into that?

question_menu.text: Sure! What do you want to know more about?

finish.text: Of course! Thanks for checking it out. Hopefully you see how engineering can be about people just as much as machines.

bye.text: No problem! Keep looking around, and come back if you want to learn more about the ergonomics setup.
